# The Subcutaneous Implantable Cardioverter-Defibrillator: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

The implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) is a cornerstone of sudden cardiac death (SCD) prevention in patients at risk of life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias [1]. While the transvenous ICD (TV-ICD) has dramatically reduced arrhythmic mortality, transvenous leads remain a principal source of long-term complications, including lead fracture, insulation failure, venous occlusion, and systemic infection [2,3]. Lead-related complications and the morbidity associated with transvenous lead extraction prompted the development of an entirely extrathoracic system: the subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) [4].

## Design and Rationale

The S-ICD consists of a pulse generator implanted in a left lateral pocket and a parasternal subcutaneous electrode, avoiding intravascular and intracardiac access entirely [4,5]. By eliminating transvenous leads, the S-ICD circumvents the venous and endocardial complications inherent to conventional devices and may reduce the risk of systemic bloodstream infection in the event of pocket infection [3,6]. The first clinical experience, reported in 2010, demonstrated reliable detection and termination of induced and spontaneous ventricular arrhythmias [4]. Regulatory approval followed in Europe and, in 2012, in the United States [5].

## Clinical Evidence

The pivotal IDE study and the EFFORTLESS registry established the early safety and efficacy of the S-ICD, demonstrating high rates of conversion of induced ventricular fibrillation and acceptable complication profiles [5,7,8]. Pooled analyses of these cohorts confirmed durable performance over intermediate follow-up, with low rates of device-related complications and effective treatment of spontaneous episodes [7,8]. 

The landmark PRAETORIAN trial provided the first randomized comparison of the S-ICD with the TV-ICD in patients with a guideline indication for an ICD but without a need for pacing [9]. The S-ICD was noninferior to the TV-ICD with respect to the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [9]. Longer-term follow-up of PRAETORIAN confirmed sustained noninferiority [10]. The UNTOUCHED study further demonstrated low inappropriate shock rates in a contemporary primary-prevention population, attributable in part to improved programming with enhanced discrimination algorithms and conditional shock zones [11,12].

## Patient Selection and Screening

A fundamental limitation of the S-ICD is its inability to provide long-term bradycardia pacing, antitachycardia pacing (ATP), or cardiac resynchronization [13]. Consequently, the device is unsuitable for patients with pacing indications or those with monomorphic ventricular tachycardia readily terminated by ATP [13,14]. Appropriate patient selection requires preimplant electrocardiographic screening to ensure an acceptable sensing vector and minimize the risk of inappropriate shocks due to T-wave oversensing [14,15]. Automated screening tools and attention to QRS-T morphology have improved candidate identification [15,16]. The S-ICD is particularly attractive in young patients, those with channelopathies such as Brugada syndrome and long QT syndrome, patients with prior device infections, and individuals with limited or no venous access [16,17].

## Inappropriate Shocks and Complications

Inappropriate shocks, predominantly due to T-wave oversensing and supraventricular arrhythmias, were a notable concern in early experience [7,18]. Dual-zone programming, the SMART Pass filter, and refined sensing algorithms have substantially reduced inappropriate therapy [11,12,18]. Other complications include pocket infection, electrode-related issues, and suboptimal defibrillation thresholds requiring repositioning [8,19]. Compared with TV-ICDs, the S-ICD demonstrates fewer lead-related complications but a potentially higher rate of nonlead complications such as wound issues [19,20].

## Implantation Technique and Evolution

The intermuscular two-incision implantation technique, replacing the original three-incision approach, has improved cosmesis and reduced complications [21,22]. Optimal generator and electrode positioning, confirmed by the PRAETORIAN score derived from chest radiography, predicts defibrillation success and has reduced reliance on routine defibrillation testing [23,24].

## Special Populations and Future Directions

The S-ICD has been studied in pediatric and congenital heart disease populations, hemodialysis patients, and those with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, with favorable results [25,26,27]. A major limitation—the lack of pacing—is being addressed through the integration of the S-ICD with leadless pacemakers in a modular, communicating system, with early studies demonstrating successful ATP delivery [28,29]. Ongoing refinements in device size, battery longevity, and sensing further enhance its role [30]. Current guidelines recommend the S-ICD as a reasonable alternative to the TV-ICD in patients without pacing requirements [1,13].

## Conclusion

The S-ICD represents a meaningful advance in SCD prevention, offering protection from ventricular arrhythmias while avoiding the risks of transvenous leads. Randomized evidence confirms its noninferiority to the TV-ICD for appropriately selected patients [9,10]. Careful screening, optimized programming, and emerging combinations with leadless pacing are expanding its applicability and may further define its place in contemporary device therapy [28,30].
